title: Holographic heat engines for Schwarzschild black holes
abstract: We construct reversible black hole heat engines in asymptotically flat spacetime using quasi-local gravitational thermodynamics. We enclose a Schwarzschild black hole in a finite spherical cavity and identify the working substance with the dual thermal system on the cavity boundary. The surface pressure and boundary area define a thermodynamic pressure-volume pair in the dual system, while all coupling constants of the gravitational theory remain fixed. We derive exact efficiencies for the Carnot, Otto, Diesel, Brayton, and Stirling engines and compare them numerically. These efficiencies probe the quasi-local equations of state of the black hole. The regenerated Stirling efficiency remains remarkably close to the Carnot bound and approaches it in the high-temperature limit.
summary: This paper develops a framework to analyze reversible heat engines powered by black holes confined within a cavity using quasi-local gravity. By mapping the black hole's thermodynamics onto standard P-V and T-S diagrams, the authors derive efficiencies for various cycles. The key finding is that the regenerated Stirling efficiency approaches the Carnot limit at high temperatures, providing insights into the fundamental thermodynamic constraints imposed by gravitational systems.
main_problem: The study constructs reversible black hole heat engines operating within a finite cavity using quasi-local gravitational thermodynamics.
main_result: Exact efficiencies for standard heat engines (Carnot, Otto, etc.) are derived, showing that the regenerated Stirling efficiency approaches the Carnot bound in the high-temperature limit for the large branch.
method: The analysis employs the quasi-local formalism to define thermodynamic potentials (E, S, P, V) on a boundary enclosing a Schwarzschild black hole. Standard thermodynamic cycles are then mapped onto these gravitational variables to calculate efficiencies.
model_or_system: The system models a four-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole enclosed in a spherical cavity ($r_B$). The working substance is dual to the thermal system on this cavity boundary, allowing for the application of classical thermodynamics concepts (P-V, T-S diagrams).
key_observables: Engine efficiencies ($\eta$), heat transfers ($\delta Q$, $\delta W$), and thermodynamic potentials derived from quasi-local gravity.
important_parameters: The analysis is restricted to the large black hole branch for stability; high-temperature limits ($T_h 	o \infty$) are crucial for comparing with Carnot bounds.
main_assumptions: The construction assumes asymptotically flat spacetime and relies on a quasi-local description of gravity, requiring specific boundary conditions (e.g., 'flat-space background subtraction').
figures_summary: Figures illustrate constant-property paths (P-V and T-S) for both the large and small black hole branches, detailing how different strokes traverse the thermodynamic space.
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives fundamental thermodynamic relations using quasi-local gravity, then applies these relations to calculate efficiencies for various standard heat engine cycles. The focus culminates in a detailed comparison of the regenerated Stirling cycle efficiency against the Carnot limit in the high-temperature regime.
why_interesting: While focused on general relativity, the rigorous application of classical thermodynamic cycles (Carnot, Stirling) to a gravitational system provides a powerful analogy for understanding energy conversion limits in complex physical systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems thermodynamics.
